statement: For a given complex Hermitian matrix M (or general square matrix M) and a non-zero vector x, the Rayleigh quotient R(M, x) is defined as R(M, x) = (x^* M x) / (x^* x), where x^* is the conjugate transpose of x (or R(M, x) = (x^T M x) / (x^T x) for real symmetric M and vector x).

symbols.meaning: square matrix (typically complex Hermitian or real symmetric)
Rayleigh quotient of matrix M with respect to vector x

properties.property: Scale invariance: R(M, cx) = R(M, x) for any non-zero scalar c.
properties.why: The scalar factor c^* c cancels from both the numerator and denominator: ((cx)^* M (cx)) / ((cx)^* (cx)) = (c^* c / c^* c) * ((x^* M x) / (x^* x)).

properties.property: Rayleigh–Ritz bounds: for Hermitian M, R(M, x) in [\lambda_{\text{min}}, \lambda_{\text{max}}], with equality attained at the corresponding eigenvectors v_{\text{min}} and v_{\text{max}}.
properties.why: The Rayleigh quotient can be expressed as a weighted average of eigenvalues (\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i y_i^2) / (\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2), where y_i = v_i^* x are coordinates in the orthonormal eigenbasis.

properties.property: Critical points are eigenvectors: the stationary points of R(M, x) subject to ||x||^2 = 1 are the eigenvectors of M, and the corresponding stationary values are the eigenvalues.
properties.why: Setting the gradient of the Lagrangian L(x) = x^T M x - \lambda (x^T x - 1) to zero yields Mx = \lambda x.

properties.property: Decomposition as sum of squared cosines: for covariance matrix M = A'A with orthonormal eigenvectors, R(M, x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i (x' v_i)^2 / (x' x).
properties.why: Vector x decomposes on the eigenvector basis as x = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i v_i with projection coordinates \alpha_i = (x' v_i) / (v_i' v_i).

properties.property: Range contains the spectrum: for any matrix M, the range of R(M, x) is the numerical range and contains the spectrum of M.
properties.why: For Hermitian matrices, the numerical radius equals the spectral norm, and \lambda_{\text{max}} is the spectral radius.

properties.property: Expectation value in quantum mechanics: R(M, x) represents the expectation value of the observable corresponding to operator M for a system in state x.
properties.why: In quantum mechanics, state observable expectation values are evaluated by the normalized inner product (x^* M x) / (x^* x).

properties.property: Operator recovery via polarization: for fixed M over the complex field, the map R(M, x) completely determines M via polarization; over real scalars, it determines only the symmetric part of M.
properties.why: Quadratic forms over complex vector spaces uniquely determine the underlying matrix, whereas over the reals they only determine the symmetric part.

assumptions.breaks_when: x = 0, causing division by zero in the denominator x^* x.

assumptions.assumption: Matrix M is complex Hermitian (or real symmetric) for real-valued bounds and eigenvalue extremization.
assumptions.breaks_when: M is non-Hermitian, which may yield non-real values for x^* M x and non-orthogonal eigenvectors.

assumptions.assumption: Dimensions of matrix M and vector x are conformable (M is n x n and x is n x 1).
assumptions.breaks_when: Vector dimension does not match matrix dimension, causing inner products and matrix-vector multiplications to fail.

failure_modes.cause: Evaluating the Rayleigh quotient at the zero vector x = 0.

failure_modes.signature: R(M, x) produces non-real complex numbers or values outside [\lambda_{\text{min}}, \lambda_{\text{max}}]
failure_modes.cause: Matrix M is non-Hermitian, so x^* M x is not guaranteed to be real.
Length of vector x does not equal the column/row size of matrix M.
